We introduce a new mathematical framework, known as cluster character, which is specifically tailored to tackle questions arising from the study of Fomin--Zelevinsky's dualization approach to classical and quantum cluster algebras. In our research, we establish a direct connection between the cluster characters of the affine classical Dynkin diagrams and the finite-dimensional irreducible representations of quantum groups. This relationship yields several significant consequences, including the derivation of formulas for the dimensions of the irreducible representations of quantum groups and the demonstration that the Weyl character formula is attainable within the framework of cluster characters. Additionally, our approach provides an alternative proof for Kostant's multiplicity formula from the perspective of cluster algebras.

Recently, pyramid scams have shifted from traditional methods to utilizing blockchain technology, posing significant challenges to their detection and prevention. To address this, our research takes a closer look at the Forsage scheme, uncovering its underlying structure and analyzing how it evades conventional pyramid scheme recognition tools. We discovered that Forsage operates as a multi-level Ponzi scheme rather than a typical pyramid, leveraging complex affiliate relationships that can be difficult to pinpoint using conventional methods. By delving into the intricacies of Forsage, we highlight areas where current detection techniques fall short and provide suggestions for their improvement in the fight against emerging scams.

The VVV survey's extensive and deep photometry allows for a more precise identification of the most promising globular cluster candidates within the galactic bulge. By re-analyzing the VVV survey data through a combination of differential photometry and isochrone matching using the Dartmouth Atlas, we have refined the characteristics of 19 potentially distinct globular clusters. Our study reveals 7 new clusters that may not be previously reported, and confirms 12 clusters identified by other researchers. We estimate the galactic coordinates, radii, and luminosity ranges for these 19 clusters, and compare our results with other studies that used the 2MASS and OGLE-III survey data. We also discuss the possible membership for 5 clusters that exhibit distinct populations within the galactic bulge.

In this context, we explore a subclass of holographic tensor networks known as "hyper-invariant MERA," which can be applied to simulate a wide range of systems through simple bond updates, potentially mimicking power-law behaviors exhibited by quantum systems. By developing a precise theoretical model, we were able to demonstrate the effectiveness of hyper-invariant MERA in capturing the characteristics of critical Ising models displayed in a semi-tensorized renormalization group representation. Notably, this approach allows for a deeper understanding of why tensor network algorithms based on invariance often yield accurate results for these types of systems. Furthermore, we show that hyper-invariant MERA can be optimized to reproduce the results of semi-numeric approaches and provide a more precise explanation for the widespread success of these methods.

Understanding and predicting complex business processes through time-series data is a challenging task that has been explored using various deep learning methods in recent years. Due to the lack of publicly available information about how these techniques are being applied in operations research, this study seeks to compare and analyze leading deep learning approaches for process-based data. It delves into the mathematical representations and predictive performance of state-of-the-art methods such as Graph Attention Network, Recurrent Transformer, and their hybrid counterparts for contextualization and forecasting tasks. By examining the impact of model parameters and contextual information, this study aims to provide operations research practitioners with valuable insights and actionable knowledge for selecting suitable deep learning techniques for their specific applications and processes.

In this research, a key concept is the Gelfand-Shilov space, denoted by $\Sigma_{\theta}$. Its Fourier transform characteristics are examined for a specific $\theta$ value, showing that the non-degenerate character of $\Sigma_{\theta}$ is linked to the smoothness of its underlying function. A major finding is that for $\sigma \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with compact support, the property $\sigma \in \Sigma_{\theta}$ is not intrinsic in itself when examining the composition of the Fourier transform and the Hermite operator, thereby providing a distinct perspective on the operator $\mathcal{H}$ and the space $\Sigma_{\theta}$. As a result, a class of Toeplitz operators is shown to be non-ordinary within the context of $\Sigma_{\theta}$.

A new method has been implemented to simulate the extreme distribution of radiation within the near-ultraviolet spectrum associated with the massive AD Leo eruption in 1985. This eruption, classified as a huge superflare, released an extremely high amount of energy, 10 to the power of 32 ergs, and was primarily observed in the ultraviolet and X-ray spectra. The simulation utilizes a radiative hydrodynamic model to recreate the radiation profiles and temperatures associated with the flare, and it is particularly well-suited for simulating the intense heating and subsequent cooling phases of solar flares. By incorporating the effects of radiative cooling and the influence of convection on the radiation, the model successfully replicates the distribution of radiation across the ultraviolet spectrum for the 1985 eruption of AD Leo, and it is also applied to a lesser flare event occurring the same day to demonstrate its utility.

Neural networks with point-based inputs have gained significant traction due to their versatility in processing complex, irregular data.  However, the current pool of point-based networks lacks a proper mechanism for input smoothing, which is a common preprocessing technique that enhances network performance by mitigating noise and dimensional effects.  To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel smoothing method tailored specifically for point-based networks, leveraging transformation-dependent smoothing components that effectively reduce noise and dimensional effects.  Our approach, referred to as TPC (Transformation-Based Point Cloud smoothing), is particularly efficient in handling challenging low-data scenarios.  Experimentally, TPC outperforms existing methods across a range of point-based networks on five benchmark datasets for 3D object classification, generation, and segmentation tasks.

Using the RPA method, we derived the complex Jost function for $^{16}$O's giant dipole resonance, which includes both real and imaginary components of the energy in the complex energy plane. By analyzing the derived function's properties, we were able to explain the resonant width and shape of the $^{16}$$O$'s GDR within the RPA framework. Our results demonstrate that the RPA method is capable of accurately describing the $^{16}$O GDR in the complex energy plane. We also observed that the RPA framework is composed of both stable and unstable components of the $^{16}$O GDR. Our analysis revealed that the complex energy plane's property of analytic continuation enables us to recover the width of the GDR by employing an energy contour that is suitable for $^{16}$O, and that the RPA framework's stability at high energies is necessary to describe the $^{16}$O GDR accurately. Our research further found that the $^{16}$O GDR's center energy is only minimally affected by the RPA framework's smallest unstable components, whereas the RPA framework's largest unstable components significantly affect the width of the GDR. Our analysis of the complex energy plane's derivative of the logarithmic RPA potential revealed that the $^{16}$O GDR's width is primarily influenced by the RPA framework's most unstable components that reside within the GDR itself.

This research develops an innovative method for grouping similar trajectories from complex systems by leveraging the information already present in their data. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on linear or second-order methods, the proposed technique utilizes parabolic models to detect and group analogous time courses. Following the methodology development, we apply this technique to achieve two objectives: enhancing the effectiveness of wound healing simulation models by accurately categorizing their parameters, and streamlining time courses from identical underlying systems by accounting for noisy measurements in the data.

Generative adversarial networks can generate highly realistic data, and opponent models in economics simulate the behavior of rival entities. By combining these concepts, GANs can be used to generate synthetic data consisting of two parts: a genuine sample from a primary distribution and a response from an opposing agent. We introduce SparseGAN, an opponent agent model that incorporates sparsity constraints, allowing for the elimination of unnecessary features in generated text. Utilizing a latent space, SparseGAN effectively combines sparsity constraints and opposing agent behavior through opponent modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SparseGAN in comparison to opposing agent models and standard GANs through evaluation on text creation tasks, showcasing improved performance according to various metrics.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, interstellar panspermia, has been a hypothesis for over a century. To investigate the potential for this to occur within our solar neighborhood, we analyze the characteristics of interstellar gas and dust that could affect the viability of microbial life transported on comets and meteoroids. We examine the effects of cosmic and gamma-ray radiation, as well as the chemical composition of comets and meteoroids, on the survival of extremophilic microorganisms. We also consider the paths that comets and meteoroids take through the solar neighborhood and their likelihood of being carrying life. If we assume that life can be preserved for a decade or less, we find that approximately 0.01% of comet/meteoroids that pass through the solar neighborhood could be carrying life. However, this percentage could be influenced by a variety of factors including the distribution of comets and meteoroids, their orbital characteristics, and the conditions of the interstellar gas and dust. If we assume that life can be preserved for longer than a decade, the percentage of comet/meteoroids that could be carrying life is significantly higher.

Animal abundance estimates obtained through Capture-Recapture methods can be enhanced by incorporating information on species-specific resource preferences. This synergy can be achieved by utilizing models that account for both capture probability and resource selection probability, leading to a new method for estimating population density. Our study presents a theoretical Capture-Recapture resource selection modeling framework for inferring local density from capture data, with the aim of exploring its statistical properties. Furthermore, we have developed an algorithm for capturing recovery histories, and have conducted extensive simulations to assess the performance of this algorithm under various scenario assumptions. The results obtained from these simulations are discussed in the findings section of the study.

The study of multilayer networks has become a valuable tool for examining complex systems across various fields, including neuroscience, economics, and climate dynamics. Current research often focuses on single-layer networks, overlooking the significance of multiple layers in capturing interconnections between different layers. We address this shortcoming by developing a new approach for analyzing the dynamics of phase oscillators within multilayer networks and applying it to solve a specific problem related to signal transmission through these networks. The transmission solution reveals how the dynamics of phase oscillators are affected by the interconnections within the network, and we demonstrate the practical utility of our method by simulating and comparing a single-layer network and a multilayer network featuring the same connections between nodes in different layers. The transmission solution we derived for the multilayer network yields identical results to those obtained for the single-layer network when used in the same simulation.

In this work, a novel method for stress determination through the use of the Cauchy stress function is proposed. By defining the stress function as the solution to specific partial differential equations, we derive the associated fundamental solutions for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional cases. The proposed method leverages the concept of the Riemann function, incorporating the Laplace operator and its higher-order equivalents. By setting the stress function as the product of a potential function and a polynomial, we demonstrate the ability to obtain explicit formulas for both linear and quadratic potential cases. The resulting expressions for the stress tensor as well as the displacement field are provided, offering a straightforward and minimal parametrization approach.

In program verification, establishing connections between source code properties and execution behavior relies heavily on program examination, a challenging task that requires efficient algorithmic solutions. We introduce a new principle, the geometric principle for program examination, which provides a solid foundation for understanding the fundamental requirements of program examination. By analyzing the principle's components, we can gain insights into the limitations and potential extensions of program examination. The principle is presented in a general and abstract manner, applicable to various program verification contexts, including but not limited to the specific method for program examination presented in section 2.

Consider the group $G=PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ acting on the upper half-plane $\mathcal{H}$ through the identity component $\Gamma_0(4)$ of the Kleinian group defined by four real points. Let $\mathfrak{X}_\mathcal{H}$ denote the space of smooth functions on $\mathcal{H}$ with the Poisson algebra $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{H})$ and unitary dual $\widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{H})$. For any unitary character $\chi \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{H})$, define the representation $\pi_\chi$ as the restriction of the action of $G$ on $\mathfrak{X}_\mathcal{H}$ to the invariant subspace $\mathcal{P}_\chi(\mathcal{H}) = \{\phi \in \mathfrak{X}_\mathcal{H} : \chi(\phi) = \chi(\phi)\circ \gamma \text{ for all } \gamma \in \Gamma_0(4)\}$. Accurate node positioning in wireless networks relies on reliable metric collection. However, the presence of malicious nodes can significantly compromise location estimation techniques. This research investigates small-world graph-based estimation methods and finds that, in contrast to traditional network models, it can demonstrate robustness against malicious nodes, specifically showing that accurate positioning is achievable even in the presence of an extensive network compromise, up to $\Omega(n^{\gamma-1})$ where $\gamma$ represents the scale-free graph's exponent and $n$ the network's size.

Understanding traffic congestion and detecting incidents such as crashes and construction are crucial components in developing intelligent transportation systems. Current approaches to traffic state estimation primarily rely on models that incorporate historical data and machine learning techniques but lack effectiveness for incident detection in the short term. This paper presents a non-parametric method to estimate traffic conditions on unknown roads within a few hundred kilometers without prior knowledge of the road. Specifically, we develop a robust, accurate approach to detect incidents and assess traffic congestion sizes in real-time, excluding biased estimates. The proposed method leverages unique characteristics of traffic and employs a combinatorial technique known as integer programming to detect incidents on frequently traveled roads. We evaluate and refine the approach using real-time floating car data from the Tokyo metropolitan area and find it to be highly accurate in detecting incidents and estimating congestion sizes on frequently traveled roads in urban areas.

Numerical simulations in general relativity are heavily limited by the quality of initial data and the accuracy of time-evolution methods. To overcome these limitations, we've developed the Conformal Traceless Teukolsky-De Wit-Hu method to directly solve the Einstein wave equation in the conformal field, bypassing the need for a spacetime metric. This approach allows for relaxed boundary conditions, greater flexibility in generating initial data, and more precise control over numerical errors in the time-evolution process. We've successfully applied the CTTK method in numerical simulations of dynamic black hole mergers and found that it offers significant advantages over traditional techniques, particularly in accurately capturing post-merger remnants and with a lower computational cost.

The Nernst effect refers to an electromotive force generated in a conductor by applying heat to one end and cooling the other. This effect is usually accompanied by an associated magnetothermoelectric phenomenon known as the magnetothermoelectric Nernst effect or the Nernst phenomenon, which involves cross-interactions between temperature, magnetization, and electric fields. This phenomenon has a distinctive "Nernst-like" signature in magnetothermoelectric measurements and has been observed thus far in ferromagnetic materials with long-range order. In this study, we observe the Nernst phenomenon in thin layers of the ferrimagnetic, disordered material Mn$_3$NiN. These layers exhibit a peculiar behavior where the Nernst phenomenon is strongest at the point of minimum magnetization, an unexpected result given the usual correlation between magnetic order and Nernst effect in ordered materials. By theoretically modeling this phenomenon using a Boltzmann transport equation, we find that the unusual behavior of the Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN layers can be attributed to the disordered nature of this material, which results in the strongest scattering of conduction electrons occurring when the magnetization is minimum. This leads to the scattering of thermal electrons, increasing the Nernst effect in this material. Integrating AI into user-centered systems through efficient, high-capacity interfaces is a pressing need, given the rapid growth of data processing requirements and the need to minimize physical infrastructure. This collaboration can take various forms, including cloud-based services, big data analysis, and AI training. To address the significant performance limitations of current interfaces, this research leverages theoretical modeling and real-world experimentation to explore the potential gains of using 64GB DDR3 RAM in user machines, with results showing notable improvements in system performance, exceeding 5 times in certain scenarios. Furthermore, this work identifies key factors influencing efficiency at user ends and offers practical guidelines for optimizing system productivity.

We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions for a class of nonlinear, non-autonomous integro-partial differential equations subject to artificial barriers imposed on their solutions. These equations feature sub-diffusive behavior and are defined on a torus. Our main results include the convergence of solutions to the corresponding equations without barriers, as well as estimates for the rate of this convergence.

We provide a new approach to determining the congruences of 2-dimension al Galois representations in the context of weight one and exceptional binary cubic fields. This involves utilizing Kummer theory to establish connections between the Galois module of a specific binary cubic field and the Galois representation associated with an Eisenstein polynomial, thereby revealing the structure of the associated Selmer group and ultimately the congruences it satisfies. This methodical approach also yields an alternative proof for the non-existence of weight one forms for GL_2 in the context of CFT.

Consider the boundary $\partial \Omega$ of a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. The problem investigates the properties of a measure $\mu$ defined on $\partial \Omega$ with respect to isoperimetric configurations and optimal solutions for a variational problem with a constraint on the mean curvature of the boundary. It is proven that the measure $\mu$ is minimized among all isoperimetric configurations with fixed volume and enclosed measure $\mu$ for $n=2,3$. Additionally, the equality case in the second-order variational criterion is examined to determine its implications for a measure defined on the boundary of a domain with prescribed properties, including a specified enclosed measure and mean curvature.

A recent study used electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to map harmonic contours in a 2D self-sensing composite material with a known, simple electrical properties structure. Researchers were able to precisely determine the exact shape of a material contour subject to an unknown external harmonic force, successfully sidestepping issues related to property calibration. A novel method leveraging evolutionary algorithms was developed to accurately pinpoint the contour's precise location and shape, and subsequent simulations demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach.

We're exploring the fundamental question of whether highly intelligent individual components are beneficial for achieving high overall performance in a complex system. To address this, we'll examine various examples from biology, psychology, and engineering, searching for patterns and exceptions that can guide our understanding. It's essential to note that our primary focus is on the underlying principles rather than applying these examples for analogical reasoning in other fields.

In this work, we establish a connection between the tensor representation of a Euclidean space and its geometric properties, specifically using the concept of measures that define a scalar quantity based on the inner product of a vector with itself. We examine the metric, norm, and duality measures in this context and explore their relationship to the scalar product. For a Euclidean space with a symmetric positive definite matrix as its tensor representation, we find that its geometry can be fully determined by the set of its eigenvalues if the matrix is diagonalizable. We also investigate the properties of this set, which we call the measure spectrum, and discuss its applications in the fields of mechanics, optics, and electronics.

If we consider that the weak neutral force is tri- or even quad- factorial rather than the well-established trifactorial nature, it's possible to explain the absence of observed neutral currents in taste experiments using a simple assumption that durational coherence is limited to the weak time frame. This concept can be applied to neutral particles that affect taste and could potentially be detected in low-energy experiments, offering a unique approach to searching for extensions to the Standard Model through neutral current interactions. This method can be used to reinterpret existing data from experiments such as the Brookhaven E805 and LEAR using an upgraded version of the TPC detector, along with potential for similar searches at existing facilities like J-PET, BES III, and CLAS12.

Building upon the Toda conformal quantum field theory, specifically within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT, we establish the fundamental Ward identities associated with the shift operator $\mathsf{S}_0$ using the conformal three-point functions of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT. These identities are then utilized to derive the general form of the three-point function $\mathsf{S}_0(\xi_1,\xi_2;\xi_3)$ for primary fields with zero conformal weight. Notably, this result confirms a conjectured formula proposed by Hakimi and Hikihara. Additionally, we extend the Ward identities to the class of quasi-primary fields within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

To create a comprehensive understanding of the brain's functional architecture during physical activity, it is necessary to investigate the ambulatory state that corresponds to each type of movement and the corresponding neural signals. Previous studies using electroencephalography (EEG) have explored this relationship for sedentary and walking states but have been limited in their ability to differentiate between various movements. In contrast, EEG's more advanced counterpart, electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals, offer enhanced spatial and temporal resolution, making them a superior choice for this research. This study utilized ECoG signals obtained from two subjects who walked on a treadmill while their brains were being recorded. By applying a variety of signal processing techniques, we were able to extract beta-frequency brain activity from the recorded data and create a 3D visual representation of the results. This visualization showed that different brain regions corresponding to various movements exhibited distinct patterns of activity. Furthermore, we were able to identify specific frequencies associated with each movement, including walking, running, and climbing stairs, and even break them down into their individual step cycles. This research sheds new light on the complex interplay between the brain and the body's physical activity and provides a method for decoding the step frequencies from the recorded ECoG signals.

We investigate the subgroups of a right-angled Artin group that are comprised of elements with a specified property, focusing on the division into subgroups of a particular type. Specifically, we seek to characterize the collections of subgroups of a right-angled Artin group G (for a given graph Δ) whose intersection within G is also a right-angled Artin group. Our analysis reveals that these subgroups that intersect to form a right-angled Artin group can be equivalently defined as those whose corresponding vertices in Δ are pairwise connected by paths in Δ, forming a tree. This equivalent condition is a key outcome of our study.

Connecting variables in multivariate time series represents the relationships between elements in a system over time, offering a richer view than static connectivity methods like correlation or Granger causality. However, computing and storing vast matrices of time-dependent connections is computationally expensive and requires significant memory. In this work, a novel method for efficiently obtaining the connectivity at each time step is developed, reducing the input to just the distance matrices across all time steps for a given variable. These distance matrices serve as input to a recurrent neural network that outputs the connectivity at each time step for every element in the system. The proposed method is not only computationally and storage-efficient but also robust, as demonstrated through connectivity smoothness-based stability metrics in various examples, including a synthetic dataset, EEG recordings during a memory recall task, and EEG and fMRI recordings from a language processing experiment. The proposed technique is an affordable solution for examining the dynamic connections within complex systems.

A living organism's presence can be indicated by its movement, which is a key element in images and video frames containing biological specimens.  This problem has various applications, including bioterrorism, illegal wildlife trading, and environmental monitoring.  A method is presented here to automatically detect movement caused by living creatures.  It employs the GIF-based Outlier Detection (GOD) algorithm, which identifies anomalous areas of image frames indicating creature movement.  The GOD method's effectiveness is tested and compared to alternative methods, demonstrating its superiority in biologically relevant image analysis.

To enhance the efficiency of Monte Carlo methods, particularly through GPU acceleration, our research focuses on optimizing the Monte Carlo simulation by reducing the computational time for advanced ordering in the RIMIC method. Our study begins by reviewing the RIMIC algorithm and an improved ordering technique for Monte Carlo simulations. We then develop two advanced ordering methods: a direct descendant ordering and a hybrid ordering technique. The results of our experiments using the Stuttgart Monte Carlo Method Suite show that our new ordering methods significantly outperform the existing implemenation by reducing the average CPU time by approximately 20 times. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the GPU acceleration of the RIMIC method can achieve speeds on par with the current state-of-the-art GPU Monte Carlo methods in the Stuttgart Monte Carlo Method Suite.

Topological phases play a significant role in the study and application of exotic materials. Topological insulators, which were initially discovered, have various analogs, including their three-dimensional forms and topological crystalline insulators. A specific class called the Topological Anderson Insulator (TAI) was theoretically proposed to possess unique topological properties protected from disorder. Nevertheless, the TAI concept has faced skepticism and controversy, primarily arising from its proposed realization in one-dimensional form being questioned and the absence of a well-defined topological parameter in its original proposal. This study introduces a robust and well-characterized topological Anderson conductor in three dimensions, utilizing random binary perturbations as scattering phases. It demonstrates the topological stability of this phase, even in the presence of strong disorder, and identifies key signatures in spectroscopic and transport measurements to identify this phase. Notably, our findings show that strong scattering phases serve as the most suitable means of realizing robust topological properties in three-dimensional materials, thereby providing a solid foundation for the TAI concept.

This study focuses on supersingular elliptic curves from a specific genus one curve category, defined as curves with a high j-invariant and low endomorphism count in characteristic two. A key feature of these curves is their inability to be reduced to a single isogeny layer. As a result, they require a second isogeny layer to reach a point of stability from which all other curves can be reached via a single isogeny layer. A key tool used to study these curves is Bley-Verruel's connection to a certain category of polynomials, specifically those representing genus one curves that can be expressed as a sum of two quadratic polynomials with no common factors. A key result of this research involves establishing upper and lower bounds on the number of trims, defined as distinct isogeny layers, which can be reached from a given curve via a single isogeny layer. Additionally, this research provides estimates on the number of trims for a randomly selected curve from the supersingular elliptic curve family in characteristic two.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the number of intricate Higgs parameters exceeds the number of independent variables, with many being highly correlated. As a result, it's necessary to employ a reduced parameter set when studying Supersymmetric phenomena through Higgs boson production and decay in the MSSM. This analysis outlines the intricately connected parameters relevant to the $CP$ properties of Higgs couplings with fermions within the MSSM, focusing on lighter quark and charged lepton interactions. Variations in effective Higgs couplings are examined as a function of intrinsically defined parameters, with notable effects seen in $h^{\pm} \to ta^{\pm}$ and $H^0 \to b\bar{b}$ decay patterns. Furthermore, this study highlights potential Higgs physics signatures at the Large Hadron Electron-Positron Collider and the Large Hadron Collider, including rare decay modes of light neutral Higgs bosons and enhanced production rates for stop pairs mediated by the lightest neutral Higgs boson.

In large-scale multi-agent systems like online advertising, learning agents are often situated in different environments with variables like user response patterns and resource constraints that vary greatly from one another. Typically, researchers assume that the environment parameters are shared among the agents or are known in advance. For agents in real-world applications, however, such shared knowledge is not always feasible due to its extensive requirement for mutual information exchange. This research addresses this fundamental issue by introducing the concept of distributed situational linear bandits, a framework in which agents that share a common parameter estimation method operate independently within individual environments. Theoretical findings are also presented, including a lower bound and upper bound on regret after N time steps, which reflects the impact of the diverse environments and the extent to which the agent's model is in line with the actual environment.

We appreciate the diverse range of opinions from discussants that have enriched our understanding of DTGL methods, particularly in relation to several critical assumptions made in our previous work. In response to these comments, we'd like to address several key concerns and provide additional insights into several important issues that have been raised. Specifically, we'll be examining the scope and limitations of our previous results, as well as exploring the implications for several important special cases. In addition, we'll be presenting a new result that addresses the difficulty of learning from fully labeled data in the presence of label switching, and providing a more comprehensive analysis of the risk bounds for both risk-neutral and risk-averse settings.

Our study investigates the potential for event shape engineering at the LHC using inclusive distributions from Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_\rm{NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Event selection is based on transverse momentum cuts for charged particles within the pseudorapidity range $2.4 < \eta < 4.8$. We examine the response of the system to variations in centrality, transverse momentum thresholds, and event charge balance. Our findings demonstrate that average charged particle momentum is directly proportional to the event's geometric eccentricity in most cases, exhibiting an exception for the most central collisions (10-5%). Furthermore, we observe that the event's elliptic flow is influenced by the transverse momentum threshold only for transverse momenta less than 1.5 GeV, and that the system's elliptic flow is directly proportional to the event's charge balance. We discuss the implications of these results on the partical coherence length within the Quark-Gluon Plasma.

When considering interference networks with multiple transmitters and receivers, determining the extremal gain per unit bandwidth is crucial for optimizing performance. This gain can be achieved through various power management techniques, including the use of binary thresholding, optimal, and random, methods. In general $K$-user interference networks, the extremal gain achieved via optimal power management is found to be significant, exceeding that of binary power management by an amount proportional to $\sqrt{K}$. Conversely, in networks with a single transmitter and receiver, the performance difference between optimal and binary power management is found to be minimal, showing that the $\sqrt{K}$ benefit is a critical mass effect that requires multiple transmitters and receivers. This research confirms the theoretical benefits of optimal power management in multiple-antenna networks and provides a lower bound on the performance improvement achievable with optimal power management in single-antenna networks.

This study introduces a novel integration approach for simulating multiple particles interacting via elastic collisions. By accurately capturing the intricate details of particle interactions, we leverage high-resolution simulations to model a wide range of phenomena, from the behavior of individual particles in random flows to particle-filled turbulent fluids. The proposed integration method employs a combination of the Verlet scheme and a second-order predictor-corrector algorithm to efficiently track particle trajectories over extended periods. The study's findings demonstrate that this method delivers precise and stable results, outperforming existing integration techniques for simulations involving multiple time steps and close particle encounters. The accompanying code is designed to be adaptable for various numerical integration methods, allowing users to easily experiment with alternative approaches. The research's focus on the flow of granular materials served as a testing ground for the method, yielding a $10^3$ to $10^4$ fold improvement in computational efficiency when using 25 $\mu$s time steps. The developed code's modular design enables seamless integration of new numerical techniques, paving the way for further optimization of the simulation code.

This article presents an investigation into the Diophantine equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, focusing on solutions where $a$, $b$, and $n$ are whole numbers. Building on the findings of Brown and Goldstine, we establish a lower bound for $n$ in terms of $|a|_7$ and $|b|_7$, and further demonstrate that $n$ must exceed the sum of the 7-adic absolute values of $a$ and $b$. Additionally, we provide examples illustrating that the proposed $n$ lower bound is both necessary and sufficient to solve for $a$, $b$, and $n$ within the $\mathbb{Q}_7$ field.

Our research focuses on simulating and improving a monopod jumping model that accurately accounts for the mechanical properties of the ground it lands on. Leveraging our understanding of how the ground's behavior affects sound waves generated during impact, we've developed a computational method to test various design changes for enhanced jumping performance, with a focus on how the ground's response influences the acoustics of the impact. Sensitive analysis revealed that the jumping height is affected by ground stiffness, with a notable increase in heights achieved on softer grounds, while the sound waves produced during impact are more sensitive to the angle of approach and ground density. By integrating our simulation results, we've created an interactive jumping performance visualization that demonstrates the relationship between the monopod's design, the ground it lands on, and the acoustics of the impact.

In this paper, we re-examine the concept of meson shape factors within a quark-diquark picture. By re-defining these factors, we demonstrate their utility in a more general context, suitable for both mesons with orbital excitation and those without. Our approach is shown to be equivalent to the original quark models for both $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ meson states. Furthermore, we provide a clear and consistent description of the internal structure of mesons with both even and odd orbital parity.

Hierarchies within information systems have specific characteristics that require a well-defined, linear progression from a general, all-encompassing category to increasingly specialized subcategories. Existing model-based approaches often overlook the inherent structure of these relationships, instead focusing on functional connections between data components. This research presents an innovative concept for creating expandable models that explicitly incorporate the inherent structure of information system hierarchies, using UML as a foundation. The proposed method incorporates specific notation for representing hereditary relationships and hierarchical boundaries, and applies this concept to UML's sub-languages, SBD and OOR. The utility of this approach is demonstrated through the development of an expandable model for calculating hereditary hierarchies within information systems, incorporating the principles of descriptive logic.

Quantum annealing has been successfully applied in solving a variety of optimization tasks within the "precise cover problem," though the suitable duration of its annealing schedule has not been thoroughly examined. Utilizing a simulated quantum circuit and accurate cover problem formulated with random matrices, our study finds that the optimal quantum annealing interval is directly proportional to the standard deviation of the eigenvalue spectrum for a particular matrix, which characterizes the sample's dynamics during a quench induced by a sudden change from the initial quantum state of the annealer to a classical state, mimicking the effect of an uncompleted annealing process. Our findings are verified across various sample sizes and spectral gap widths, and may serve as a guideline for efficiently determining the suitable duration of the annealing schedule in experiments.

We present a dual-band model containing two energy bands to analyze the screening properties within infinite-layer nickelate materials. By establishing a clear connection to the parent M{\o}lmer-Kunz-Thomsen (MKT) Hamiltonian, we derive an effective Hamiltonian for both the hole and electron-like bands. Our calculations demonstrate that the MKT Hamiltonian results in both bands being equally populated, and we determine the effective Hamiltonian parameters through screening calculations within the $e_g$ and $t_{2g}$ bands to understand the physics of this material. By applying the MKT Hamiltonian to infinite-layer nickelate, we aim to provide a well-defined and well-understood framework for this unique class of materials featuring both strong correlation and doped M{\o}lmer-Kunz-Thomsen physics.

The characteristics of dense hadronic matter, particularly its sound speed, are analyzed within dense stellar matter. Quark-gluon plasma is compared to dense hadronic matter at high densities of strangeness-bearing particles. Two models, the chiral perturbation theory and the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, are employed to calculate sound speeds in dense hadronic matter. A range of density ranges are examined, including densities relevant to neutron stars. The results from the two models are found to converge at high densities of dense hadronic matter. A key finding is that the sound speed in dense hadronic matter approaches one-third the speed of light as matter becomes increasingly dense. This information is utilized to calculate the maximum mass of neutron stars, which is found to be 1.8 solar masses.

We have derived a comprehensive operator identity that represents the evolution of a quantum state under the influence of a Markovian dynamics governed by a generic Liouvillean superoperator, specifically we used the compass model as a test case. This operator identity was utilized to demonstrate the validity of a previously proposed theoretical prediction, which describes the asymptotic behavior of a generic quantum state when subjected to a repeated application of a compass system's dynamics. We have analyzed the limits of this state's properties as it undergoes successive interactions with the environment and found that, in the limit where the system's interaction with the environment is weak, the state's lowest and highest occupation number components become distinct, with the middle component disappearing in this limit. We have further investigated the effects of an initial shift of the compass system and found that it results in the mixing of the lowest and highest occupation number components of the state.

A significant phenomenon in protoplanetary disks, vertical shear instability (VSI), can be influenced by the presence of dust. To understand this interaction, we examined VSI in the outer areas of a disk using both analytical and numerical methods. Our analysis showed that the effectiveness of VSI is reduced when the ratio of gas to dust density falls below a certain threshold. We found this reduction in stability occurred when the rotation curve of the disk deviates substantially from a linear state and when the VSI becomes combined with an inner, more unstable layer. Notably, the inner layer's instability in this context is similar to that reported in previous studies of VSI within the disk. The exact threshold for reduced stability is difficult to pinpoint due to the limitations of our numerical model in accounting for the inner layer's behavior. Nevertheless, our results consistently indicate that the reduction in stability occurs at a gas-to-densities ratio of less than 100, although the precise value cannot be determined with our current simulation capabilities.

This research focuses on harmonic maps between a bounded domain with a variable scalar curvature and a domain with a uniform bound on its growth, specifically within the class of functions with a limited upper curvature. We begin by establishing the non-compactness of maps from the domain to a space with a bounded curvature, and further demonstrate the absence of infinitely growing boundary mappings by utilizing the Schaeffer boundary regularity theorem in conjunction with a non-compactness criterion. Additionally, we provide an exploration into the properties of harmonic maps with a variable scalar curvature within the class of functions with a polynomial upper curvature.

In recent years, neural networks with dynamic architectures have significantly outperformed their fixed counterparts in various tasks. particularly for the Attention-based networks that are widely used now days. One area where dynamic architecture has shown great potential is in the context of fully connected layers, specifically within the Fully Connected Attention Mechanism. However, one major limitation of these networks has been their difficulty in handling input with different channel sizes due to their rigid architecture. To address this challenge, we propose a novel module called Global Mean Pooling Dynamic Entrance (GMPDE) that is capable of adapting to inputs of any channel size while simplifying the fully connected attention mechanism. In addition to its versatility, GMPDE has been found to significantly reduce computational costs when compared to its attention-based counterparts. Our proposed approach has been extensively evaluated and has shown superior performance in multiple applications, including sound classification, image classification, and natural language processing.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements from a space telescope like Gaia are susceptible to a small effect from general relativity, specifically in the determination of nearby star distances. By incorporating the most recent post-Newtonian calculations, we have investigated the influence of PPN $\gamma$ variation on parallax measurements and found that a deviation of 10^-3 in $\gamma$ could lead to a 0.01 milliparsec uncertainty in the measurement of a star with a 10 microarcsecond parallax. Consequently, we estimate that a value of $\gamma$ cannot be reliably determined from parallaxes with an accuracy better than 0.3 times 10^-3 during the Gaia mission, until the uncertainty in parallaxes drops below approximately 0.3 milliparsec.

To improve the comprehension of vast amounts of everyday knowledge represented in question-answer pairs, a new method called Coarse-to-Careful (C2C) is proposed for reinforcing the semantic connections within existing pre-trained language models. C2C builds upon the foundation of existing semantic inference methods by incorporating a diverse set of questions that connect two pieces of knowledge in a variety of ways. Connections between knowledge are represented as a pathway between the two relevant pieces of information, which are then used to determine the appropriate question type, effectively guiding the model's understanding of the connected knowledge. Our evaluation of the proposed framework across multiple question-answering benchmarks demonstrates enhanced performance, particularly in accurately answering questions that connect two different pieces of knowledge. The results of our extensive experiments using SStQA, ComplexQA, and Natural Questions demonstrate enhanced performance across various evaluation metrics.

To advance the comprehension of molecular electronics and valence bond coupling, a comprehensive study is conducted on the most well-established data of comet spectra, specifically focusing on oxygen-containing molecular cations. Although cometary analysis provides highly reliable, albeit deficient knowledge, it is necessary to integrate these results with more developed theoretical models involving molecular orbital and Hamiltonian calculations. This study addresses the lack of information regarding comet-based measurements of comet spectrum analysis, particularly the positions and intensities of spectral features. Specifically, no previous research has been done on the position and shape of comet spectrum's low-energy feature, and only a limited number of studies exist on the bonding versus antibonding spectral features. As a result, a more comprehensive and precise theoretical comet spectrum is obtained for the simplest oxygen-containing molecular cations, including CO, O$_3$, CO$_2$, H$_2$O, OH, and O$_3$2. These results demonstrate the significance of both bonding and antibonding orbital coupling for this class of molecules and provide a precise explanation for the pre-ionization state of comet spectra, often considered mysterious. Additionally, this research highlights the value of deficient comet data integrated with more advanced theoretical models, and the importance of measuring the position and shape of comet spectrum's low-energy feature.

Federated learning has gained significant interest for training models using user-generated data across diverse networks. However, recruiting participants from various demographics often encounters difficulties in achieving a high participation rate, resulting in typically narrow and homogeneous datasets being utilized for training. These limited datasets lead to decreased model performance and generalizability in real-world applications. This paper introduces a novel random stroll approach in federated learning, allowing for the efficient incorporation of extremely diverse data. In this method, participants take random steps in the model parameter space during training, effectively exploring different subpopulations efficiently. We develop an optimization framework tailored for heterogeneous datasets and demonstrate the random stroll method's efficacy by applying it to multiple challenging tasks, including imbalanced classification and partially supervised learning. The resulting algorithm yields comparable, and in some cases superior, performance when compared to cutting-edge approaches on various benchmark datasets.

Research examining the link between mental health treatment within the penal system and recidivism rates among offenders who undergo such treatment has yielded inconsistent results. Prior studies have failed to account for selection bias, which is a significant limitation according to meta-analytic reviews. Using Danish register data from 2004 to 2014, this paper investigates the relationship between mental health treatment ordered as part of a prison sentence and future offending behavior among prisoners, with a focus on psychosocial functioning and future crimes. To address concerns about selection bias, the analysis employs propensity score matching to compare prisoners who were ordered to undergo mental health treatment to those who were not. The study finds that prisoners who were required to receive mental health treatment had improved psychosocial functioning and lower future offending rates compared to those who were not. Notably, this positive effect on future crimes is observed among prisoners who completed their treatment orders. If we assume that completion of treatment orders is indicative of prisoners who are more likely to adhere to treatment, then this finding suggests a positive impact of treatment on future crimes among this subgroup of offenders. If we take a more neutral view of treatment completion, then the results may be influenced by selection bias. The study also finds that prisoners who were required to receive mental health treatment had higher future incarceration rates if they had a shorter prison sentence, which could be related to the type of treatment they were ordered to undergo or the factors that led to their shorter sentence.

To improve healthcare image segmentation, there's a growing interest in using unlabeled images for better performance, which has led to a surge in semi-supervised methods. Despite the potential for significant benefits from using extensive, readily available but unlabeled images, researchers have had limited success in utilizing them. One major restriction on the use of unlabeled images stems from the complicated and often unreliable predictions they produce from deep learning models, which can hinder the usual strategy of training with them for consistency. This paper presents an unconventional yet straightforward approach to incorporate unlabeled images by training the model to accurately predict the already unknown pixel classifications. The technique is simple, doesn't require any additional parameters or complex computations and has been tested on two well-known healthcare image segmentation datasets, demonstrating its capability to achieve high-quality results with significantly reduced reliance on labeled data.

To tackle the intricate challenge of analyzing complex quantum dynamics through Liouville space, we have developed a graph neural network (GNN) protocol that utilizes a straightforward, interpretable approach to capture the underlying dynamics. By representing the Liouville space as a structured and symbolic graph and incorporating a minimal set of fundamental neural network components, our method efficiently extracts valuable information from the high-dimensional data associated with the Wigner function. By applying this technique to a highly entangled, many-body spin system and a one-dimensional Koch model, we obtained striking results that demonstrate the significance of incorporating spatial information through the GNN protocol. Notably, our research showed that the simple neural network architecture is capable of accurately reproducing the outcome of the chaotic quantum system for a remarkably long period of 1000 time steps. Moreover, we discovered that the obtained neural network weights exhibit a well-defined relationship with the underlying Hamiltonian, providing a unique perspective on the quantum dynamics. These novel insights are expected to pave the way for a deeper comprehension of the intricate quantum chaos by focusing on the fundamental properties of the neural network weights.

Consider a mixture model where we have $m$ component distributions, denoted as $f_1, \ldots, f_m$, and their corresponding weights are $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_m$. The goal is to estimate the weighted average of the population parameters from a single-component distribution, $\theta_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \pi_i \theta_{ji}$, using the maximum likelihood estimation method. However, one major constraint is that the individual weights $\pi_i$ are not known. We propose an alternative method to estimate the weighted average parameters $\theta_j$ by utilizing the maximum likelihood estimation for the average parameters from a Dirichlet distribution with a known diffusion matrix $D$ and an unknown matrix $\Theta$, which specifies the weighted average parameters for each component distribution. The proposed method results in an assessment for the average weighted parameter $\hat{\theta}_j$ for each $j$, along with an associated standard error $\hat{\sigma}_{\theta_j}$. Furthermore, we discuss two distinct scenarios for the weights $\pi_i$: one where they are known and another where they are unknown and estimated separately. The proposed method is computationally efficient and does not rely on iterative optimization procedures. We provide theoretical proofs of the asymptotic normality of $\hat{\theta}_j$ for both known and unknown weights $\pi_i$. Knowledge tracing, an essential component in Intelligent Tutoring Systems, aims to forecast a student's next action or answer based on their historical behavior. Recent advancements in knowledge tracing utilize deep learning techniques, yet evaluating and selecting these models remains challenging due to limited student data. Presently, methods for evaluating knowledge tracing systems rely on outdated information, such as accuracy for the next action, which fails to consider the time-sensitive nature of student actions. This issue becomes even more critical under emerging tutoring settings such as real-time streaming data. To address these challenges, we've developed pyKT, a Python-based framework tailored for evaluating knowledge tracing systems. This framework introduces novel evaluation metrics, including the time-aware knowledge tracing metric, to account for the sequential nature of student actions. Furthermore, it provides utility functions to perform cross-validation and evaluate models using streaming data. PyKT is an open-source platform available on GitHub, designed to facilitate research and development in knowledge tracing through its simple and extensible API.

Let $\Omega$ be an unbounded open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and consider the space $C_0^{\infty}(\Omega)$ of functions with compact support in $\Omega$. For an elliptic differential operator $P$ that is not identically zero, we prove that $P$ does not extend to a bounded operator from the Soblev space $H^{k}(\Omega)$ to $H^{l}(\Omega)$ for $l$ greater than $k+2$. This result can be seen as a consequence of the lack of compactness of $\Omega$, and we also demonstrate a related property for operators on compact manifolds with boundary.

Creating a consistent proof for a theorem 1.0 \live in universe U is only possible if there are no contradictions within U, as demonstrated by the existence of a contradictory clause, known as a Skolemization of $\neg\phi$, resulting from $\phi$ live in U. However, proving $\phi$ in U for a given $\phi$ that isn't already disproven involves constructing a proof for 1.0 given $\phi$ in U, which we refer to as a proof certificate for $\phi$ in U. Our proposed format,.smt(e) evidence, is an extension of.smt(e) with additional features for capturing the original problem context, including theories, sorts, and function symbols, and a clearer definition of what it means to prove a given formula. We have successfully applied this format to resolve various verification challenges, leveraging existing SMT solvers without the need for problem-specific tuning or native support for proof generation. Our evidence format and accompanying tools are part of the Alethe project, which aims to provide a universal framework for presenting and comparing different proof formats used by various verification systems.

As mobile devices have become ubiquitous, Federated Learning has emerged as a prominent technology to train AI models without transferring private user data. Despite its advantages, the method is limited by the need for synchronized data transfer from participants, which can lead to significant delays due to varying reporting frequencies from contributors. In response, researchers have explored ways to speed up the process by allowing uncontrolled data updates from participants, but this approach is subject to significant drawbacks, such as accelerated model divergence, risk, and security breaches resulting from unchecked gradient submissions. This study tackles this challenge by developing a risk-controlled Federated Learning method, known as Buffered Synchronous Aggregation, which enables secure and efficient AI model training despite unregulated gradient submissions from participants. The innovative technique uses unapproved gradients in the aggregation process and mitigates potential risks through careful selection and delayed aggregation, resulting in significant performance enhancements in real-world experiments, outpacing existing Federated Learning benchmarks by up to 13%.

Recently, massive amounts of publicly available data have fueled the progress of speech recognition technology. To extend speech recognition capabilities to low-resourced languages, we explore transfer learning approaches using data from linguistically related, high-resourced languages. This study leverages massive amounts of data from a linguistically similar language to enhance ASR systems for another language, without requiring any native data for the target language. To accomplish this, we develop a two-stage approach where speech recognition is performed on a high-resourced language, using a model trained on a different, high-resourced language. We then use the intermediate results to train an ASR model for the target language, incorporating phonetic unit refinement to account for linguistic differences. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we develop and test ASR systems for two low-resourced languages using data from a linguistically related, high-resourced language. The results show significant improvements in recognition accuracy for both languages.

To enhance the navigation capabilities of marine robots in dynamic and unpredictable environments, it's crucial to incorporate knowledge about the time-varying nature of these settings. This approach is essential for adapting to changes that occur over a short period. This paper presents a novel navigation system for marine robots that leverages a unique Gaussian Process model to capture the variability of their surroundings over time. The proposed method Leverage a sparse representation to efficiently handle long-term stability and focus on modeling rapid temporal changes. The effectiveness of this system is demonstrated through simulations of a dynamic and ever-changing ocean environment, as well as real-world testing with a freely floating marine robot. The results show that this approach achieves comparable performance to traditional methods while utilizing significantly less information about the environment.

We employ a 1.5-ADC (1.5-Advanced-Dictionary-Based-Coordinate) method to redefine the metrics of rotating, non-uniform two-fluid celestial bodies in General Relativity. This approach allows us to recast the metrics in a uniformly convenient format for both compact and expanding configurations. By conducting a thorough review of previous work, we also examine the relationships between various ADC frameworks. Furthermore, we clarify the connection between the 1.5-ADC and 1.5-PD frameworks.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Rectification methods focus primarily on developing highly sophisticated models without much consideration for practical applications. In contrast, we take a more practical, real-world approach by incorporating practical domain conditions, specifically few-shot domain transfer, into our GER model. Leveraging the principles of meta-learning, we create a versatile model capable of rapidly adapting to new domains with limited information. Our proprietary token type system and weighted reconstruction loss function further enhance the model's performance in new domains. In our experiments, we achieve superior results on the IELI test set, a widely-used benchmark for evaluating the language learning ability of artificial neural networks. Our approach also demonstrates significant improvements over traditional domain adaptation methods in various transfer settings, including those with limited data.

The task of allocating scarce items to self-interested, rational agents in a cooperative game is examined in this study, with the goal of ensuring that the outcome is fair and stable according to the Pure Nash Equilibrium (PNE) criterion. To address this challenge, a framework for determining whether a proposed allocation is PNE-equitable is developed and made easy to check, and this is used to create PNE-fair allocations for a wide range of cooperative games through a series of straightforward steps. The study also explores several well-known cooperative games and demonstrates how PNE-equitability can be efficiently achieved for each one. Furthermore, a rigorous analysis into the PNE-equitability of mechanisms for distributing items to players in a variety of settings is provided. The study's findings are accompanied by PNE-equitable allocation algorithms for a broad class of preference domains, and a thorough discussion on the relationship between PNE-equitability and other desirable properties is presented.

UGC 8839, an extremely faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a compact, HII region spiral pattern. Using the Hubble Space Telescope, we obtained high-resolution, color images of UGC 8839, allowing for a detailed examination of its structure. The HII regions are primarily located in the inner region of the galaxy, where we found a stable disk component by fitting the Hubble Space Telescope observations with a three-component model, consisting of an extremely faint bulge, a disk with varying surface brightness, and the HII regions themselves. The results reveal a consistent rotation curve for the disk, with a maximum rotation speed of approximately 45 km/s and a corresponding stellar mass of 3.1 x 10 to the 9th power M sun, which is insufficient to create the HII regions on its own. Therefore, we conclude that UGC 8839 contains a substantial amount of dark matter, accounting for nearly the entire rotational curve, similar to the Milky Way galaxy.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of pion properties through two-current matrix elements has been conducted, providing a comprehensive understanding of hadron structure. Two-current matrix elements, which are related to various nucleon scattering processes, have been computed for a variety of proton momentum grids. By comparing these results with a recent study on the proton, researchers have established a clear pattern of similarities and differences in the grid of two-current correlations within pions. Unlike the proton case, the pattern of two-current correlations in pions reveals distinct asymmetry in the spatial distribution of quarks, which may be linked to unique properties of pions as mesons.

For the second year of observations, the PENELLOPE campaign at the VTT, combined with the GRIS at the AAT, monitored the accretion variability of the young star XX Cha using Ca II spectroscopy and continuum photometry. With 104 sets of observations spanning one year, we found a high frequency of variable patterns in XX Cha, with the star showing a distinct preference for accretion bursts in the second half of the year. These findings challenge previous assumptions that the distribution of accretion bursts on XX Cha are random and evenly distributed throughout the year. We also determined the range of accretion rates for XX Cha as the highest ever recorded for a classical T Tauri star, which may be attributed to the minimal influence of spots on the star's overall brightness.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
socially intelligent systems. Typically, models require positive interactions
between agents as training data, but this restriction limits practical
application due to the abundance of negative experiences in real-world
scenarios. In contrast, we propose a groundbreaking method called Trajectory
Attention Model (TAM) that learns from incomplete data, focusing on completed
agent trajectories resulting from interacting pairs. TAM employs an attention
mechanism and value function estimation to prioritize meaningful trajectories
and assign credit to appropriate agents within them. The model is designed to
handle both single-agent and multi-agent challenges, with the ability to
utilize partially supervised data for training. Experimental evaluations on
publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with
TAM achieving superior performance compared to standard offline learning methods.

We developed a novel approach to align MV images obtained from different modalities. Our method employs a U-Net architecture to fuse MV images, which are treated as 3D volumes due to their limited depth. We used a combination of translation, rotation, and shear transformations to define our image alignment task as finding the optimal 2D/3D transformation and image weighting for superposition of the MV volumes. We began by training a separate U-Net for each task: calculating the 2D/3D transformation and determining the image weighting factors. We then combined two identical U-Net architectures to obtain the alignment results. We tested our method on simulated and real-world data, showing its effectiveness with mean absolute error (MAE) values of 1.01 cm and 1.41 cm for the water equivalent thickness (WET) and x-ray density (XD) maps, respectively. We also compared our approach to conventional methods, demonstrating its superior performance.

The perception that genuine nonlocal effects require true correlations between multiple particles has been challenged. Here, we demonstrate that single-particle states with appropriate preparation procedures can exhibit genuine nonlocality, as detected through the Valente et al. test for nonlocality. The validity of our approach is ensured by confirming that these states satisfy the requirements for containing no classical-quantum nonlocality or entanglement. The role of the single-particle state's environment in generating this effect is also examined, in addition to the necessity of an unambiguous distinction between the system and environment. The importance of our findings is further highlighted by the fact that they can be experimentally implemented using both continuous-variable nonlocality and discrete-variable nonlocality.

The integration of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) and education systems is a growing trend, with significant potential benefits. However, as IoV technology continues to evolve, ensuring the security and scalability of education platforms poses new challenges. To address these challenges, a blockchain- enabled, federated education framework for IoV could provide a reliable and efficient solution. Consequently, research on this topic is gaining momentum, with an emphasis on exploring novel techniques for secure, collaborative learning in IoV applications. Despite the increasing interest, there is currently a lack of comprehensive research on this subject, with most existing studies focusing on individual aspects of IoV education systems. Consequently, there is a pressing need for integrated research that considers the interplay between IoV technology and education platforms. Consequently, the need for an overarching framework that enables secure, collaborative learning in IoV applications has given rise to research on a blockchain-enabled, federated education framework for IoV. Notwithstanding the growing interest in this area, the amount of published research remains limited, with most existing studies isolating individual components of IoV education systems rather than examining the interplay between IoV technology and education platforms. Consequently, the majority of the existing literature falls within individual silos rather than an integrated IoV education framework. V392 Persei, classified as a small classical nova, experienced a significant outburst in 2018. Observations from the All-Sky Gamma-Ray Imaging Array and the Gamma-Ray Burst Observer revealed the presence of novel nova remnants emitting high-energy radiation at the site of V392 Persei. This discovery represents the first detection of a small classical nova's remnant through gamma-rays and provides a unique opportunity to study this type of object using high-energy radiation. By analyzing pre-outburst X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the X-ray Satellite, researchers found that V392 Persei's outburst was likely powered by a 0.69-day orbital period rather than the previously reported 0.65 days. The study suggests that the outburst's energy source was likely a combination of accretion in the white dwarf and an external explosion induced by the nova, rather than the nova itself. Furthermore, researchers found that the outburst showed a high degree of radiative efficiency, similar to that of recurrent novae, with an estimated peak luminosity of 6.5 x 10 to the power of 43 erg per second in the hard X-ray band and the potential for a gamma-ray jet or a highly radiative and gamma-ray luminous nova.

Codebook selection and feedback encoding in FDD systems heavily rely on channel state information obtained through pilot transmission. This information is used to create a codebook that matches the current channel conditions, thereby ensuring efficient data transmission. However, due to the limited duration of pilot transmission, the codebook selected might not always be the most optimal one. This issue is more pronounced in scenarios with rapidly changing channels. This research proposes two innovations to enhance codebook selection and feedback encoding. Firstly, we recommend dividing pilot transmission time into two segments, with the primary purpose being codebook selection and the secondary purpose being for precise CSI acquisition. This allows for the development of a codebook that accounts for the statistical characteristics of the channel, thereby reducing the search space for the most suitable codebook. This approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios with rapidly changing channels. Secondly, we propose a Precoder Selection and Feedback (PSF) algorithm that employs a Gaussian Mixture Model to describe the distribution of precipitation matrices. This approach leads to a significant reduction in the number of codebooks that need to be searched through, thereby decreasing the computational load. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approaches in various scenarios.

When applying a strong magnetic field to a three-dimensional Hofstadter model, we've found that nonequilibrium conditions can lead to the formation of sturdy, asymmetrical current patterns at the surface of the system, despite the absence of defects within the interior. These currents can flow in unique directions, determined by the interplay between the strength of the magnetic field and the nonequilibrium condition. We've characterized this behavior by calculating how the currents change in response to variations in the magnetic field, as well as the asymmetry of the nonequilibrium condition. Our results reveal that the system enters a stable, nonequilibrium state when the driving force is greater than a certain critical value, and we've also identified how the phase transitions associated with this state are affected by the orientation of the nonequilibrium condition.

The rate of change in black hole mass is controlled by two key laws: the classic von Neumann-Weiss generalization of the second law of thermodynamics, stating that mass reduction occurs at a rate greater than the rate of area decrease in the event horizon, and the Bondi mass reduction law, which describes how mass changes over time on a spacetime slice. This paper proves that under specific conditions, the Bondi mass reduction rate must be less than half the rate of the area of the event horizon, providing a wider understanding of the laws that govern black hole evolution, and offering implications for the behavior of black holes in scalar-field driven collapse.

We have performed comprehensive simulations for the formation of early, massive, compact stellar systems using a variety of theoretical models, then applied a detection-based GWEMPIRE code to search for gravitational waves emitted by these systems as they produce supernovae and compact remnants through their evolution. Our results show that even the most massive nuclear star clusters should contain at least one neutron star, and likely several, and that they should emit a wide range of gravitational waves through the mergers of these neutron stars and black stars. The expected rate of such events is highly dependent on the metal content of the system and the presence or absence of a central supermassive black hole, but even the most optimistic estimates place it well below the detection limits of LISA and AdvLISA.

In wireless communication systems, ensuring the security and reliability of data transmission is critical. Against eavesdropping attacks, the integrity of the physical layer is a key concern. This study focuses on a specific scenario - an AF relay wireless communication system that uses multi-carrier technology. To analyze this scenario, we first establish a mathematical framework for a single-subcarrier scenario, followed by a multi-carrier analysis utilizing diversity techniques. To enhance security in the single-subcarrier case, we develop a novel scheme that utilizes partial bandwidth to counter jamming attacks. For the multi-carrier scenario, our analysis highlights the effectiveness of diversity techniques in preventing eavesdropping. To further investigate this, we derive a threshold value that indicates the point at which the eavesdropper's reception becomes significantly impaired, thereby preventing eavesdropping. To obtain this result, we apply a new intercept probability concept that we believe has value in its own right for evaluating the security of wireless communication systems.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant challenge in utilizing these games lies in gathering sufficient data to train large-language-model-based agent architectures due to their time-consuming nature.
Typically, a trillion parameters model requires a massive 32-GPU setup and takes around 90 hours to train on a relatively small dataset of 13 million steps.
To address this issue, we've created TextWorldExpress, a high-performance text-based game emulator that can process over one million moves per second on a single GPU.
This emulator enables the efficient training of large models on text-based games by reducing the training time to around 12 hours for a similar dataset.

To enhance the efficiency of LSTM-based video recognition systems in both computation and energy consumption, a co-design approach for both algorithms and hardware is proposed in this research. Initially, a method is presented to optimize the LSTM algorithm, involving the use of a minimal amount of hidden state cells while maintaining the current feedforward and recurrent connectivity structures. To further reduce memory access and improve energy efficiency, a custom PIM (Processing-In-Memory) architecture is then developed for the designed algorithm.
